report_title: HEXANE / Lyceum (G1001) Actor Intelligence Pack — Stage-1 CTI Extraction
source: MITRE ATT&CK G1001 (https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1001/); SecureWorks CTU 'LYCEUM Takes Center Stage in Middle East Campaign' (2019, https://www.secureworks.com/research/lyceum-takes-center-stage-in-middle-east-campaign); ClearSky 'Siamesekitten – Lyceum' (Aug 2021, https://www.clearskysec.com/siamesekitten/); Kaspersky/Securelist Lyceum reporting (Oct 2021); Accenture/ESET Marlin & Shark reporting (Nov 2021, https://www.welivesecurity.com/)

actor.name: HEXANE
actor.attribution: Iran-nexus cyber-espionage group active since at least 2017; targets energy, oil & gas, telecommunications, aviation and ISP organizations across the Middle East and Africa. TTPs resemble APT33 and OilRig but victimology and toolset differentiate it as a distinct cluster.

key_campaigns.name: LYCEUM Middle East campaign (DanBot)
key_campaigns.summary: Campaign against Middle Eastern oil & gas and telecommunications organizations using the DanBot backdoor, which supports both DNS-tunneling and HTTP-based C2. Initial access via password spraying and spearphishing with macro-laden Excel documents.

key_campaigns.name: Siamesekitten / Lyceum campaign vs. Israeli targets
key_campaigns.summary: Impersonation of a legitimate HR/IT firm via fake LinkedIn personas and a spoofed careers website to lure IT and communications personnel at Israeli organizations; delivered Milan and DanBot implants.

key_campaigns.name: Marlin / Shark backdoor campaign
key_campaigns.summary: Later-stage espionage tooling (Milan, Shark, Marlin) targeting diplomatic and technology organizations; Marlin abuses Microsoft OneDrive/Graph API for bidirectional C2 while Shark uses DNS and HTTP.

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE conducted reconnaissance against target-organization personnel, gathering identity details of employees in IT and communications roles to enable social-engineering lures.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — off-victim identity reconnaissance is not endpoint-observable; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE collected employee email addresses to build spearphishing target lists.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — email-address harvesting occurs off-victim; not endpoint-observable, hunt/intel candidate

ttps.technique_name: Gather Victim Org Information: Identify Roles
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE identified individuals in specific roles (IT, communications, HR) at target organizations to tailor its recruitment-themed lures.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — role identification via public sources (LinkedIn) is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE registered domains, some spoofing legitimate brands (e.g. a fake careers/recruitment site), for use in phishing and C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — infrastructure acquisition is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via lookalike-domain and registration monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE operated attacker-controlled DNS servers to support DanBot's DNS-tunneling C2 channel.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — adversary DNS-server acquisition is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate, though downstream DNS-tunneling (T1071.004) is detectable

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE created fake LinkedIn personas impersonating HR/recruitment staff of a legitimate company to approach targeted employees.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — fake social-media persona creation is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate via persona and brand-impersonation monitoring

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE established email accounts to support its social-engineering and phishing operations.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — attacker email-account creation is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE compromised legitimate email accounts to lend credibility to its phishing and to send messages from trusted senders.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — compromise of third-party email accounts is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE obtained and used tooling to support intrusion operations alongside its custom implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — tool acquisition is off-victim; downstream use is where detection applies, this is an intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE staged malware on attacker-controlled infrastructure (including the spoofed careers site) for delivery to targets.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — malware staging on adversary infrastructure is off-victim; intel/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE leveraged valid credentials obtained via password spraying against internet-facing services (e.g. Exchange/OWA, O365) to gain and maintain access.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — valid-account abuse is detectable via impossible-travel, anomalous-logon and first-seen sign-in analytics on authentication logs

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE sent spearphishing emails carrying macro-enabled Microsoft Excel/Office attachments (DanDrop) that dropped the DanBot backdoor when macros were enabled.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — malicious-attachment delivery is detectable via mail sandboxing and macro-content analysis at the gateway

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE lured targets to a spoofed recruitment/careers website via links delivered through fake LinkedIn personas and email.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link-based spearphishing is detectable via URL detonation and proxy telemetry to newly-registered/lookalike domains

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE relied on targets opening malicious Office documents and enabling macros to execute the DanDrop dropper / DanBot payload.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Office applications spawning script/child processes after macro enablement is a core, well-covered detectable behavior

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE induced victims to click links to attacker-controlled sites hosting malicious content.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — link clicks are detectable via URL-gateway and proxy logs; endpoint signal is indirect

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used PowerShell scripts for execution, tooling and DNS-based post-exploitation activity.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — script-block/module logging and suspicious PowerShell parenting are core, well-covered detections

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used the Windows command shell to run commands and orchestrate its tooling on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — cmd.exe execution with anomalous parents and command lines is visible in process-creation logs

ttps.technique_name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Visual Basic
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used VBA macros (DanDrop) embedded in Office documents to drop and execute the DanBot backdoor.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Office spawning script children via VBA macros is a strong, detectable process-lineage anomaly

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used scheduled tasks to establish persistence for its implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — scheduled-task creation is logged (Event ID 4698 / Task Scheduler operational) and highly detectable

ttps.technique_name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used WMI event subscriptions to persistently trigger execution of its payloads.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — WMI permanent event-subscription creation is detectable via WMI-Activity logging and __EventFilter/__EventConsumer telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE established persistence via Registry Run-key entries for its DanBot/DanDrop components.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — Run-key value creation is directly detectable via registry-modification telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE conducted brute-force attacks to obtain valid credentials for internet-facing services.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — brute-force patterns are detectable via failed-logon volume and lockout analytics on authentication logs

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used password spraying — a small set of common passwords tried across many accounts — against Exchange/OWA and O365 to obtain initial access while avoiding lockouts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — password spraying is detectable via many-accounts/few-passwords sign-in analytics and distributed failed-auth patterns (a signature HEXANE initial-access TTP)

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used a credential-harvesting tool to steal credentials from password stores on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — password-store access is detectable mainly via known-tool execution signatures and file-access to credential stores

ttps.technique_name: Credentials from Password Stores: Credentials from Web Browsers
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE deployed a tool to steal credentials saved in victims' web browsers.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — access to browser Login Data / credential stores is detectable via file-access and known-tool telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE deployed a keylogger (a PowerShell/DNS keylogger and Milan components) to capture keystrokes from targeted users.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — keystroke-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated open application windows on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — window enumeration uses common APIs with little discrete signal; hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE collected network-configuration details (IP addresses, domain) from compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — ipconfig-style recon is common but suspicious within tight process-lineage context

ttps.technique_name: System Network Configuration Discovery: Internet Connection Discovery
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE checked for internet connectivity from compromised hosts prior to establishing C2.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — connectivity checks to well-known hosts are common; meaningful in process-lineage/beaconing context

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated remote systems on the target network to support lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — host-enumeration commands (net view, ping sweeps) are detectable in command-line logs but need baselining

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE collected the current username from compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — whoami/username enumeration is common; value is in process-lineage correlation

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated active network connections on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — netstat-style enumeration is common but meaningful in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE obtained lists of running processes on compromised systems.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tasklist/Get-Process enumeration is common but meaningful in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated local group memberships on compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'net localgroup' enumeration is directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE collected host information such as OS version and machine name.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — systeminfo-style discovery is common; suspicious mainly in process-lineage context

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated files and directories on compromised systems to locate data of interest.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — file/dir enumeration is common; meaningful when correlated in process lineage

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated user accounts within the target environment.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — 'net user'/account enumeration is directly observable in command-line logs

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated domain accounts to expand access and plan lateral movement.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — 'net user /domain' and net group domain enumeration are directly observable in command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE enumerated installed software on compromised hosts, including to identify security tooling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — software enumeration is detectable in script/command telemetry; needs baselining

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used RDP for lateral movement within compromised networks.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — anomalous internal RDP sessions are detectable via logon type 10 (Event 4624) and network-flow analytics

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used compromised internal mailboxes to send spearphishing messages to additional users within the target organization.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — internal-origin phishing is detectable via mail-flow anomalies and unusual send patterns from compromised accounts

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE staged collected data locally on compromised hosts prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — local staging in temp paths is common and noisy; better as a hunt over file-write telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's tooling captured screenshots from compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — screen-capture APIs leave little discrete log signal; behavioral/EDR hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE collected email content from compromised mailboxes as part of its espionage objectives.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — mailbox access can blend with normal use; hunt candidate via anomalous mailbox-access and sync telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's implants automatically collected files and system data of interest from compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — automated collection blends with normal file access; hunt candidate via bulk file-read patterns

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE archived collected data prior to exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — archive creation of staged data is detectable via file-write and known-archiver process telemetry

ttps.technique_name: Archive Collected Data: Archive via Utility
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used utilities to compress/archive collected data before exfiltration.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — archiver utilities used against staged directories are a detectable LOLBin/staging pattern

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's DanBot and Shark backdoors support HTTP(S)-based C2 communications as an alternative to DNS tunneling.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — HTTP C2 is detectable via proxy/beacon analytics and URI/JA3 anomalies but blends with normal web traffic

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's signature DanBot backdoor tunnels C2 over DNS, embedding commands and exfiltrated data in DNS queries/responses to attacker-controlled name servers — a defining HEXANE tradecraft.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — DNS tunneling is a strong detection surface: high query volume to a single domain, long/high-entropy subdomain labels, unusual TXT/A record patterns and non-resolver DNS destinations are all detectable in DNS logs (priority detection candidate for this actor)

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE encapsulates C2 traffic within the DNS protocol (DNS tunneling via DanBot) to conceal communications and bypass network filtering.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — protocol tunneling is detectable via traffic-shape and entropy analytics on the carrier protocol (DNS), overlapping with the T1071.004 DNS-tunneling detection surface

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE routed C2 through intermediary infrastructure to obscure the true location of its command-and-control.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — proxy relays are hard to distinguish at the endpoint; network/hunt candidate

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's Marlin backdoor abuses Microsoft OneDrive / Graph API for bidirectional C2, receiving commands and returning results via a legitimate cloud service.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — C2 over legitimate cloud services blends with normal traffic; hunt on proxy/API access anomalies to OneDrive/Graph from unexpected processes

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's implants download additional tools and payloads to compromised hosts.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tool transfer over C2 is detectable via file-write-after-network telemetry and, where HTTP is used, download analytics

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE encoded C2 data (embedded within DNS labels/HTTP) using standard encoding schemes.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — encoded C2 content is detectable via encoding heuristics and entropy analysis where traffic is inspectable

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE used non-standard ports for some C2 communications.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — protocol-on-non-standard-port mismatches are detectable via netflow/firewall analytics

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE encrypted C2 traffic using symmetric cryptography to protect command and exfiltration content.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — custom-encrypted C2 defeats content inspection; hunt on beacon/traffic-shape anomalies

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE obfuscated its payloads and scripts to hinder analysis and evade detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — obfuscated content is detectable via entropy/encoding heuristics and static signatures; needs supporting context

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Command Obfuscation
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE obfuscated command-line and script content (including PowerShell and VBA) to evade detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: high — obfuscated/encoded commands are detectable via script-block logging and encoding/entropy heuristics

ttps.technique_name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Encrypted/Encoded File
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE stored payload components in encrypted/encoded form on disk to evade static detection.
ttps.detection_feasibility: low — encrypted/encoded files on disk yield little static signal; hunt candidate via high-entropy file and decode-at-runtime patterns

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE's loaders and scripts decode/deobfuscate embedded payloads at runtime prior to execution.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — runtime decode routines are observable in script-block and command-line logging

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE took steps to impair host defensive tooling to reduce detection of its implants.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — tampering with security tooling (service/registry/process changes) is detectable via service-state and registry-modification telemetry

ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE exfiltrated collected data over its C2 channel, including embedded within DNS-tunneling traffic.
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — exfil over C2 blends with C2 traffic; detectable via outbound-volume/beacon anomalies and, for DNS, oversized/high-frequency query analytics

ttps.technique_name: Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
ttps.procedure_description: HEXANE exfiltrated data to cloud-storage services (e.g. via the Marlin backdoor's OneDrive channel).
ttps.detection_feasibility: medium — uploads to cloud-storage endpoints are detectable via proxy/DLP telemetry and anomalous data-volume to cloud APIs

detection_signals: High-volume DNS queries to a single second-level domain with long, high-entropy subdomain labels (DanBot DNS tunneling) — priority detection
DNS queries to non-resolver / attacker-controlled name servers, unusual TXT/A record request patterns
Password-spraying pattern: many distinct accounts hit with a small set of passwords, distributed failed auth against Exchange/OWA/O365
Office application (excel.exe/winword.exe) spawning script/child processes after macro enablement (DanDrop)
PowerShell script-block logs with obfuscated/encoded content or DNS-query construction
Registry Run-key value creation for DanBot/DanDrop persistence
Scheduled-task creation (Event ID 4698) with script/LOLBin actions
Anomalous OneDrive / Microsoft Graph API access from non-browser/unexpected processes (Marlin C2)
Access to browser Login Data / credential stores by non-browser processes
'net user /domain', 'net localgroup', account/host enumeration in command-line logs
Outbound C2 on non-standard ports and protocol-on-wrong-port mismatches
notes: Base ATT&CK mapping is the authoritative MITRE G1001 technique set (36 techniques), enriched with well-documented HEXANE/Lyceum behaviors from named public reporting (SecureWorks CTU 2019 DanBot/Lyceum, ClearSky Siamesekitten Aug 2021, Kaspersky/Securelist 2021, Accenture/ESET Marlin Nov 2021), for a total of 64 techniques across 13 tactics. Every technique_id was verified present in this environment's bundled ATT&CK dataset via sigma.data.mitre_attack (0 invalid). Env conventions applied: defense-evasion emitted as tactic 'stealth'; Impair Defenses family emitted as T1685 under tactic 'defense-impairment'; encrypted/encoded-file emitted as T1027.013. DNS-tunneling C2 (T1071.004) is HEXANE's signature tradecraft and is marked high detection-feasibility as the priority detection surface; password spraying (T1110.003) is the signature initial-access detection surface. Attribution is Iran-nexus at MEDIUM confidence: MITRE tracks HEXANE as a distinct cluster with TTP overlap to APT33 and OilRig but differing victimology/tooling, and public reporting does not converge on a single sponsor with the same weight as the MuddyWater/MOIS case. IOCs (ips/domains/emails/hashes/cves) are DELIBERATELY EMPTY: primary vendor sources could not be fetched in this pass (SecureWorks 301-redirects to a Sophos threat-profiles landing page; ESET welivesecurity Marlin URLs returned 404), and the no-hallucinated-IOC rule forbids emitting indicators not seen in a fetched source. Raw DanBot/Milan/Shark/Marlin domains and hashes should be ingested directly from the SecureWorks, ClearSky and ESET appendices before this pack's IOC block is populated. Low detection-feasibility techniques (hunt candidates, not detection candidates): T1589, T1589.002, T1591.004, T1583.001, T1583.002, T1585.001, T1585.002, T1586.002, T1588.002, T1608.001, T1056.001, T1010, T1074.001, T1113, T1114, T1119, T1090, T1102.002, T1573.001, T1027.013.
